title: Building Resilient Platforms: Insights from 20+ Years in Mission-Critical Infrastructure
gist: American Express infrastructure head Matthew Liste (ex-JPMorganChase, Goldman Sachs) lays out 12 principles for building internal mission-critical platforms, serving ~20,000 internal developers at Amex and ~60,000 at JPMorganChase. Key specifics: the '0114' fleet-currency target (zero humans, whole fleet upgraded in under a day, every 14 days), n/n-1 version support contracts, building only regulator-required control planes on top of open source, and paying internal teams to migrate off deprecated platforms.

themes.theme: Platform scale and reliability economics in banking

insights.claim: American Express runs its credit card authorization systems at six to seven nines of availability, while systems like mobile apps tolerate more downtime; the reliability target is set by the commercial value of each platform.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Card-auth infrastructure is held to near-zero downtime, so vendors selling into it compete on reliability above cost.
insights.quote: at American Express, our credit card authorization systems, they run at six nines, seven nines.
insights.locator: 3. Use the 3 S's

insights.claim: Internal platform teams at large banks serve developer populations comparable to mid-sized software companies: about 20,000 internal developers consume Amex's infrastructure platforms and about 60,000 did at JPMorganChase.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Big-bank internal platform orgs are large buyers of developer tooling, and a meaningful market on their own.
insights.quote: at American Express, that's about 20,000 people that consume the things we build. At JPMorganChase, it was more like 60,000.
insights.locator: The Principles of Infrastructure Platforms

insights.claim: For mission-critical platforms, stability, security and scalability are non-negotiable, and cutting cost on any of them leads to failure. Spend should be controlled by choosing how many features to build, not by skimping on the three S's.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Infra budgets at regulated firms adjust by narrowing scope rather than cutting reliability spend, which supports demand for resilience tooling.
insights.quote: If you decide to get cheap on any one of these, you'll ultimately fail for this kind of software.
insights.locator: Now, to be clear, early days

insights.claim: Platforms that succeed often fail later from runaway consumption: people adopt a product they love, volume grows, bottlenecks appear, and the scaling problem turns into a stability problem.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Platform success creates the next reliability risk, so scalability has to be built in ahead of demand.
insights.quote: I've often built platforms that have worked until they didn't.
insights.locator: They don't tolerate downtime

insights.claim: Liste says banks that followed AWS's shared responsibility model and Well-Architected guidance by building multi-region were largely unaffected by the AWS us-east-1 outage.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Banks' multi-region designs reduce exposure to a single hyperscaler region failing, which weakens the case that cloud concentration is a systemic risk.
insights.quote: Very few of our banks were impacted. Why? Because they had built multi-region
insights.locator: Amazon do a really good job of this

insights.claim: Liste's '0114' standard for keeping a platform current: zero people involved (fully automated), the entire fleet upgraded in under one day, and a full upgrade cycle at least every 14 days.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: A concrete automation target that shows where enterprise infra spend goes: fleet-wide upgrade automation and patch orchestration.
insights.quote: You should have zero people involved in maintaining currency, so it should be fully automated.
insights.locator: I'll explain what that stands for

insights.claim: Where upgrades affect clients (SDKs, client libraries, API specs), platforms should set an explicit contract of supporting only the current and previous version (n and n-1), for example on a roughly three-month release cycle.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Formal version-support windows are how internal platforms copy hyperscaler deprecation discipline.
insights.quote: then you have to have a contract with the client saying, I will only support n and n-1.
insights.locator: Now your maybe major version's behind

insights.claim: Clients usually get no value from upgrading themselves, so platform owners have to make the upgrade obligation explicit and formal up front, or currency slips and major-version gaps make later upgrades disruptive.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Upgrade debt builds up by default; automation and contracts are the only reliable fixes.
insights.quote: It is not as if the clients have any value driven typically from upgrading themselves.
insights.locator: My software cycles, my platform cycles

themes.theme: Build vs. buy: open source and minimal differentiation

insights.claim: At Goldman, JPMorgan and Amex, database-as-a-service ran on open-source Postgres. The only thing built in-house was a control plane that takes regulator-required daily snapshots to object storage.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Banks build thin compliance layers on open-source engines instead of proprietary databases, which is good for managed open-source vendors and bad for proprietary DB vendors.
insights.quote: What we wrote was a control plane to do daily backup because that was required from the regulators. That was the only thing we wrote.
insights.locator: All the places I worked have database

insights.claim: Liste estimates that the vast majority of critical financial-services systems now run on open source, after the industry moved heavily to Linux about 20 years ago.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Open source is the base layer of bank infrastructure; vendor value has moved to integration, support and compliance wrappers.
insights.quote: the vast majority of our critical systems are today built on top of open source.
insights.locator: Principle 11, which is about standing

insights.claim: Open-source components such as Postgres, Kubernetes and Kafka are offered by every cloud provider, so building on them gives portability across clouds through shared semantics.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Building on open-source primitives lowers cloud lock-in for large enterprises and adds pricing pressure on hyperscalers.
insights.quote: Every single cloud provider offers a Postgres variant. They offer a Kubernetes variant. They offer a Kafka variant
insights.locator: Principle 11, which is about standing

insights.claim: Internal platforms often form when teams consolidate duplicated work. At one bank, about seven teams each ran their own enterprise-hardened Kafka until it was centralized into one managed Kafka service.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Duplicated self-managed infrastructure inside enterprises is where managed-service and platform consolidation deals start.
insights.quote: there were probably seven different teams doing Kafka in their own way
insights.locator: Most of the time platforms

insights.claim: Opinionated dev teams eventually adopt central platforms because maintaining their own Postgres, Linux distro or even compiler is a poor use of money compared with core work such as trading algorithms. Regulators provide the stick.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Regulatory compliance burden pushes bank engineering toward centralized platforms and away from DIY infrastructure.
insights.quote: writing my own compiler might not be the best way to spend my money building better trading algorithms
insights.locator: They will tell me, why should I use

themes.theme: Iterate fast: the container orchestration path

insights.claim: In the mid-2000s a bank Liste worked at adopted Linux container primitives and built its own orchestration, then moved to Mesosphere (seen at Twitter), then to Kubernetes. He says iterating instead of waiting put them two to three years ahead on containers.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Early adopters that iterate through interim tools build platform capability sooner; making clients depend on stable primitives (containers) keeps migrations manageable.
insights.quote: If we had waited for Kubernetes, we would have been two, three years later with adopting containers than we were.
insights.locator: That was pretty attractive to us

insights.claim: Migrations between orchestrators were survivable because clients depended only on the container primitive, and the platform team took ownership of migrating clients instead of leaving it to them.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Exposing stable low-level primitives and owning migrations lets platform teams switch underlying vendors without client churn.
insights.quote: how you own that migration on behalf of your clients and don't leave them saddled with that
insights.locator: That iteration was fine

themes.theme: Saying no: opinionation, tech debt and deprecation

insights.claim: Enterprise IT listens to customers worse than product companies do because internal customers are captive. Platforms should still aim at the 70-80% of needs rather than 100%.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Captive internal markets weaken feedback loops, which is a structural reason internal platforms lose to external SaaS on user experience.
insights.quote: Those of us in enterprise IT are not as intuitively trained because our customers are captive and they're stuck with us
insights.locator: Principle six, which ties into others

insights.claim: Platform builds are multi-year commitments ('puppies become dogs'). Liste has regretted platform components he is still stuck maintaining years later, so he now gates new builds harder.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Each new internal platform adds long-tail maintenance cost, which favors buying managed services over building.
insights.quote: Every platform I built has been years, even when I want to get rid of it after year one, it took me years to get rid of it.
insights.locator: Number seven, which is, be long term greedy

insights.claim: Platforms follow a speed-then-simplify cycle: race for adoption while accumulating tech debt, then slow feature velocity to strip complexity once scale arrives. Liste says he has had to do this every time.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Expect periodic velocity slowdowns at mature platforms, which creates demand for tech-debt and code-modernization tooling.
insights.quote: I'm going to slow down feature velocity, because I'm going to start focusing on removing technical debt. I've had to do that every time.
insights.locator: I have a lot of clients on it

insights.claim: Forcing clients through a forklift migration counts as a failure. When it can't be avoided, Amex-style enterprises set aside internal budget to pay consuming teams to migrate, because migration gives them no business value.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Internal migration subsidies are a hidden cost of deprecation, and automated migration tooling can capture that budget.
insights.quote: we sometimes put aside a pot of money that we give to them and say, here's money to help your developers do that
insights.locator: Internally, it's a little easier

insights.claim: Platform providers and clients have structurally misaligned incentives: once something works, clients want to stay on it forever, while the provider has to shut things off to keep the platform sustainable.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Deprecation friction is permanent, so product strategies that rely on clients moving voluntarily will underperform.
insights.quote: your incentives are not aligned with the client's incentives, usually not as a platform provider.
insights.locator: Just to state the point even more specifically

insights.claim: Platforms should 'vend ice cubes, not snowflakes': a fixed set of standard shapes with explicit shared-responsibility boundaries, instead of artisanal builds for each customer.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Standardized internal offerings mean enterprises choose platform vendors that offer fixed patterns with clear SLOs.
insights.quote: You can only vend ice cubes, not snowflakes.
insights.locator: The other aspect is also

insights.claim: Platforms should offer several abstraction layers (API, Terraform infrastructure-as-code, UI) and expose what runs underneath, such as generated Terraform and API calls, so users can debug and customize instead of hitting an opaque UI.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Transparency is now a platform requirement; IaC-native tools fit enterprise platform stacks.
insights.quote: We try and expose the Terraform, the API calls, the environment.
insights.locator: We don't obfuscate it away

insights.claim: Platform components need common observability, identity, namespaces and billing to work as a platform rather than a loose set of parts. Teams get 'freedom from choice' on these (for example, mandatory OTel) and full autonomy inside their own component.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Enterprise standardization on OpenTelemetry and shared identity SDKs entrenches open standards over proprietary agents.
insights.quote: you'll use this observability stack, you'll use OTel. You don't get to choose.
insights.locator: First of all is empowerment

insights.claim: Culture is the main lever for platform quality: teams with diverse thinking beat homogeneous ones, and leaders should actively curate team composition instead of letting teams self-select.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Leadership quality and team design are leading indicators of how well an enterprise platform org executes.
insights.quote: Every time I built monochromatic teams that all think and come from the same background, we've had worse outcomes
insights.locator: First of all is empowerment

insights.claim: Technology adoption runs quickly from impossible to magic to taken for granted. Liste cites his teenage children, who have built GenAI into everything they do.
insights.speaker: Matthew Liste
insights.so_what: Fast normalization of GenAI means expectations for AI-native infrastructure will reset quickly.
insights.quote: My kids who are two teenagers, they have completely embedded GenAI into everything they do
insights.locator: Myself, old enough to be in that bucket
